solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: One who sets police to nab young Conservative leaders at large

indicators.note: to nab is to catch hold of, so the police word holds the other letters

parts.note: cops are police

indicators.note: the leaders of the words are their first letters

parts.note: their first letters give Y and C
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large, here read as 'at large', i.e. in size large

explanation.surface: Police are told to arrest the heads of the Young Conservatives who are on the run.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter of Private Eye's crossword, so the setter is the one who sets it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclops is this puzzle's own compiler, the person who writes, or sets, the crossword.

clue.text: Wanker's "power tackle"

parts.note: p is power in physics, and on a good many switches
a ship's rig is its tackle, the gear that works the sails

explanation.surface: Some objectionable man is credited with impressive 'power tackle'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are Cyclops pointing at the schoolboy sense of 'tackle'; the wordplay wants the nautical one. Two chunks, taken in the order written.
explanation.definitionFit: A prig is a smugly self-righteous moraliser, and 'wanker' is the British insult reached for about exactly that kind of man.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Labour donor's roll laid out

indicators.note: something turned out of its proper arrangement keeps none of it, so the letters before this word come in any order

parts.note: eight letters that respell across the two entries

explanation.surface: A Labour party donor's bankroll is spread out across the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Waheed Alli, the media businessman made a peer by Tony Blair, is the party's most-discussed donor and a Private Eye regular. Fodder and definition run together with only an apostrophe between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Alli's gifts of clothes, glasses and the use of a flat to Keir Starmer made him the best-known name on Labour's donor list.

clue.text: Cabinet fail in court

indicators.note: one thing put in another ends up inside it, so the outer word splits to make room

parts.note: ct is the standard short form of court in a street address
to lose is to fail to win

explanation.surface: A whole cabinet comes to grief in front of a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' wants to be the government's and is the furniture. 'In' is the clue's only instruction, and it opens the two-letter piece rather than the four-letter one.
explanation.definitionFit: A closet is a cupboard with a door, which is what a cabinet is in the furniture sense rather than the ministerial one.

clue.text: Crafty means of monitoring 'unearthly' activities

definitions.meaning: the surface offers cunning; read as craft plus a y, it promises a vessel
the quotation marks push the ghosts-and-goblins sense, when the word only has to mean away from the Earth

explanation.surface: Something sly for keeping tabs on the supernatural.
explanation.walkthrough: The inverted commas are the tell: Cyclops flags a word he is using in an unexpected sense, and the sense he wants is the literal one. 'Crafty' hides the noun craft.
explanation.definitionFit: A space probe is an unmanned craft sent out to watch and measure what happens beyond the Earth, which is monitoring the unearthly in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Soft porn, say, is like a false tan?

indicators.note: something soft holds no shape of its own and can be pushed into any form, letters included

parts.note: seven letters, comma and all, that resettle into the hyphenated answer

explanation.surface: Soft pornography is being likened to a fake suntan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' normally tags an example and here it is fodder; 'Soft' looks like half a familiar phrase and here it is the instruction. Both words change job at the same moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A false tan comes out of an aerosol, so the adjective describing anything applied by spraying is the one that fits it.

clue.text: Rex penetrates any sort in Strand

indicators.note: to penetrate is to get inside, so the king's letter goes within the other letters
to sort is to rearrange, so the letters of any are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Rex is Latin for king, abbreviated R as in royal signatures

explanation.surface: A seedy scene: a king entering some low dive on London's Strand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' rearranges ANY to YAN, and R, for Rex, 'penetrates' it. The Strand is a famous London street, but here 'Strand' is a thread.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarn is a spun thread, so a single strand of fibre fits it.

clue.text: One's into lounge music? Sweet!

indicators.note: something put into a thing sits inside it, between the parts already there

parts.note: to loll is to lounge about
pop is the chart kind
i is the Roman one

explanation.surface: Someone owns up to a taste for easy-listening music and is told that's great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet!' is teenage slang for 'great' in the surface and a plain noun in the answer. Lounge music is a genuine genre, which is what makes 'lounge' look like part of a phrase rather than a verb on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a boiled sweet on a stick, so the bare noun 'sweet' covers it.

clue.text: see 26ac.
Conservative element getting on shelter

parts.note: someone getting on in years is old
to guard something is to shelter it, keeping it from harm

explanation.surface: The ageing Tory contingent goes looking for cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital-C Conservative points at the party, and the definition works for the entrenched wing of any body at all. 'On' belongs to 'getting on' rather than telling a piece where to sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The old guard are the long-serving members who resist change, which is the conservative element of an organisation whatever its politics.

clue.text: (&14dn.) Party aimed to break up certain Internet sites

definitions.note: plural sites for the collective noun phrase

parts.note: a social is a party or informal gathering

indicators.note: breaking something up scatters its pieces, so the letters of aimed are reassembled

explanation.surface: A political party set on dismantling some online platforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks like a political party, but here it is a social gathering; then 'to break up' rearranges AIMED into MEDIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Facebook, Twitter and similar platforms are collectively known as social media, so the phrase names a particular class of websites.

clue.text: Unconcern — one way to get 'happy ending'

parts.note: a is the indefinite article standing in for one
a path is a way through

indicators.note: the ending of a word is the single letter it finishes on

parts.note: the last letter of the first word inside the quotes

explanation.surface: One route to a happy ending is being offered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy ending' is the massage-parlour joke in the surface and a letter instruction in the wordplay. The quotation marks mark a phrase being spelt rather than meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Apathy is a flat absence of interest in how things turn out, which is unconcern.

clue.text: Obligation to help fund the Exchequer causes stress, savvy?

definitions.text: Obligation to help fund the Exchequer

parts.note: to tax someone is to make demands that strain them
savvy is practical know-how

explanation.surface: Paying your share towards the nation's accounts is a strain, get it?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savvy?' tacked onto the end of a sentence means 'understand?', which is why it reads as throwaway. The Exchequer is the British government's account at the Treasury, so the definition is where the money goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Taxability is the state of being liable to be taxed, and tax is what the Exchequer is funded with.

clue.text: Pissed to hear PM's conceit

indicators.note: pissed is British for drunk, and a drunk keeps nothing in line, letters least of all

parts.note: eight letters, the last two the usual short form of prime minister

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister is drunk, by all accounts, and rather full of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To hear' is the trap: it reads as a homophone signal and it is fodder. The trap dies on the count, because the letters of that phrase are the eight the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: In literary criticism a conceit is an elaborate figure calling one thing another, and that figure is what the answer names.

clue.text: see 11ac.
'The kicking out of old lover' convention

parts.note: your ex is the lover you used to have
a convention is a tradition, the thing always done

explanation.surface: Someone quotes a saying about throwing a former partner out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the first six words look like a saying being repeated, which hides the seam between the definition and 'old lover'. A convention here is a custom, not a conference.
explanation.definitionFit: Extradition is one state handing a wanted person over to another, which from that person's side of it is being kicked out of the country.

clue.text: What's the making of a good joke? LibDem leader, once in gaudy top

definitions.text: What's the making of a good joke?

parts.note: Tim Farron led the Liberal Democrats from 2015 to 2017, hence 'once'
the word joins the answer spelt exactly as it stands

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, so only the letter at the word's head is wanted

parts.note: the letter at the head of the word

explanation.surface: What makes a gag land? A former Lib Dem chief in a flashy shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'LibDem leader' invites you to take the initial L, and 'once' is what redirects it to a past holder of the post by first name. 'In' is not an instruction here — it is two letters, spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Timing is the comedian's term for when to land the punchline, and comics will tell you it is what makes a joke work rather than the words.

clue.text: Bob, hot air hack?

parts.note: h is hot, the letter on the tap
the word goes in whole
to hack at something is to cut it roughly

explanation.surface: A man called Bob is written off as a windbag of a journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot air' is one phrase in the surface and two separate pieces in the wordplay, and 'hack' is a reporter there and a verb here. Bob reads as a name right up to the last moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is the short blunt style cut level around the head, so it names one particular haircut rather than the general thing.

clue.text: Stalin's wretched enemy's head is toast!

indicators.note: wretched means in a sorry, broken state, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: the name Stalin; the 's reads as 'is', joining it to wretched

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of enemy's

explanation.surface: A gloating cheer that the dictator's foe is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalin's wretched' means STALIN is shuffled, together with E, the 'head' of 'enemy's'. 'Is toast' looks like 'is done for', but toast is the definition: SLAINTE is the Gaelic drinking toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Slainte, meaning 'health', is the Irish and Scottish Gaelic word said when raising a glass, which is a toast.

clue.text: A day in which ugly mob is protected by agents for the nation

indicators.note: something protected by others is surrounded by them, so it goes inside the agents

parts.note: the CIA is the US agency of secret agents

indicators.note: the mob letters go in between A and D
an ugly scene is a messy one, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: On a day when an angry crowd forms, spies keep it safe for the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agents' are American spies here, the Central Intelligence Agency, rather than salesmen or representatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambodia is a country in South East Asia, so it is a nation.

clue.text: Befitting of French money

parts.note: de is French for of, asked for by naming the language after the word
a cent is a coin, the hundredth part of a euro or a dollar

explanation.surface: Worthy of a handful of continental cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' modifies 'of', not 'money' — the instruction is to translate the preposition. Read the other way round the clue looks like one phrase about foreign currency, which is the whole of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Something decent is proper and suited to the occasion, which is what befitting means.

clue.text: Reflect aloud on having MP Anderson, reportedly, for breakfast?

indicators.note: a word said aloud is judged by its sound, and the spelling that reaches the grid can be a different one

parts.note: to reflect on something is to muse on it, and the noise that makes opens the answer

indicators.note: reportedly means as reported by ear, so it is how the name sounds that counts

parts.note: Lee Anderson is the Reform UK member for Ashfield, so his first name is the sound wanted

explanation.surface: Chewing over a certain MP's latest, out loud, at the breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are sounds rather than spellings, and neither is spelt the way you would guess until the other is beside it. Lee Anderson crossed from the Conservatives to Reform UK in 2024.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is the oat, nut and dried-fruit cereal eaten first thing, so 'breakfast' names it by the meal it belongs to rather than by what it is.

clue.text: Large immodest opening in short dress — what fun!

indicators.note: in places the large letter and the initial inside the shortened dress
short means cut off at the end, so the frock loses its last letter

parts.note: a frock is a dress
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: only its first letter is used

explanation.surface: A risqué outfit: a revealing split on a mini-dress, greeted with delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts FROCK to FROC; L for Large and I, the 'opening' of immodest, go 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A frolic is a bit of lively fun or a playful romp, so it answers the exclamation.

clue.text: Sceptic acting so crappily

indicators.note: a job done crappily comes out badly put together, and these letters are put together badly on purpose

parts.note: eight letters that resettle into a new word

explanation.surface: Someone is putting on a thoroughly poor performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and fodder sit side by side with nothing between them, so the adverb at the end is the only sign that anything is being moved. A sceptic here is one who withholds belief rather than one who denies.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnostic holds that nothing can be known either way about God, so 'sceptic' catches that doubting position squarely.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Sick of Scottish head gaining seat

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, and nothing behind it is taken

parts.note: the letter at the front of the word
a pew is the long bench you sit on in church

explanation.surface: Fed up with a Scotsman winning a place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sick of' reads as one phrase meaning fed up, and only 'of' is the joint. 'Scottish head' invites a first minister and wants a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In British use 'sick' is the noun for the vomit itself, not just the state, and that is the sense the answer matches.

clue.text: Straighten out misshapen nut that's on view

indicators.note: something misshapen is bent out of its form, so the letters of nut are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
an angle is a point of view or perspective

explanation.surface: Fixing a deformed nut that is on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on view' suggests display, but 'view' is the second piece, a standpoint, with 'that's on' only joining the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To untangle something is to free it of knots, so to straighten it out.

clue.text: (& 9dn.) Bowed and brief? Not Trump's apparent view of Giuliani

definitions.text: Not Trump's apparent view of Giuliani

parts.note: a bowed back
a brief is British slang for the barrister or solicitor acting for you

explanation.surface: Humbled and short with people — apparently not how Trump sees Rudy Giuliani.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' negates the definition, so the clue describes what Trump would deny rather than what he thinks. Both halves of the wordplay are plain synonyms, one of them slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent lawyer is a crooked one, and Rudy Giuliani was disbarred in New York over his 2020 election claims while Trump went on defending him.
